# Navier-Stokes Solvers

## Overview
This family provides numerical methods for discretizing and solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations to produce velocity and pressure fields for volumetric rendering [G]. It solves the problem of advancing fluid state over time by combining advection, diffusion, and pressure projection, distinguishing it from particle-based siblings like [Gaussian Splashing](1387-gaussian-splashing.md) and [Position Based Fluids](1765-position-based-fluids.md) by its Eulerian grid-based approach, and from pure advection methods like [Smoke Advection](4639-smoke-advection.md) by its explicit enforcement of incompressibility and viscosity [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family discretize the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a structured 3D grid, typically using staggered or collocated layouts [G]. The core mechanism advances the velocity field $\mathbf{u}$ and scalar fields (e.g., density, temperature) over a time step $dt$ through three sequential operations [G].
1. **Velocity Advection**: Transporting the velocity field by itself using the convective term $(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{u}$, often via semi-Lagrangian tracing [G].
2. **Diffusion**: Solving a linear system for viscous forces $\nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{u}$ and thermal diffusion, where $\nu$ is the kinematic viscosity [G].
3. **Pressure Projection**: Solving a Poisson equation $\nabla^2 p = \frac{\rho}{dt} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{tentative}$ to enforce the divergence-free constraint $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$, then correcting the velocity via $\mathbf{u}^{new} = \mathbf{u}^{tentative} - \frac{dt}{\rho} \nabla p$ [G].
These steps are applied per time step to maintain numerical stability and physical plausibility [G].

## Subtopics

### [Navier-Stokes Solver Components](13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md)
Provides the numerical discretization and solution steps for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a grid, producing velocity and scalar fields [G]. Chosen when general-purpose incompressible flow simulation is required, distinguishing it from fire-specific or particle-based variants [G].

### [Grid-Based Simulation](13502-grid-based-simulation.md)
Discretizes physical sources into a volumetric representation on a structured spatial domain [G]. Chosen when fixed voxel arrays are preferred for efficient divergence and advection calculations via 3D textures, distinguishing it from particle-based siblings like [Gaussian Splashing](1387-gaussian-splashing.md) and [Position Based Fluids](1765-position-based-fluids.md) [G].

### [Navier-Stokes Fire Simulation](14659-navier-stokes-fire-simulation.md)
Models fire as a hot, turbulent gas by solving fluid dynamics laws to generate time-varying volumetric data [G]. Chosen when physically accurate convection and buoyancy are needed, distinguishing it from procedural or particle-based siblings by deriving motion from conservation of momentum and mass rather than noise or ad-hoc rules [G].

### [Hybrid Particle-Level Set Method](20293-hybrid-particle-level-set-method.md)
Combines marker particles and a dynamic level set to track liquid surfaces [G]. Chosen for liquid animation requiring mass conservation and stability, distinguishing it from grid-only methods by addressing mass dissipation issues [G].

### GPU-based Semi-Lagrangian Cloud Simulation
An interactive cloud simulation implemented on NVIDIA programmable graphics hardware using a 3D grid-based solver [S1]. It incorporates cloud physics and vorticity confinement into the semi-Lagrangian solver [S1]. The 3D grid-based simulation is structured as layers of 2D textures for easy computation on the GPU [S1].

## Background
The Navier-Stokes equations, formulated in the 19th century, describe the motion of viscous fluid substances [G]. In computer graphics, their application to fluid simulation was pioneered by Jos Stam in 1999 with "Stable Fluids," which introduced semi-Lagrangian advection and stable integration schemes suitable for real-time rendering [G]. This work laid the foundation for grid-based fluid simulation in visual effects and games [G]. The family has since expanded to include specialized variants for fire and smoke, integrating thermal buoyancy and density transport [G]. GPU-based implementations, such as semi-Lagrangian cloud simulations, structure 3D grids as layers of 2D textures to leverage programmable graphics hardware for interactive evolution [S1].
